summary: Weekly POC sync to review cost/unit economics for Meridian Retail pilot. Reviewed tokens/sec/$ numbers from last benchmark, discussed caching savings from KV/prefix caching, and batching tradeoffs. Agreed to run an improved benchmark with quantized model and revised batching rules; Redwood to send updated cost model spreadsheet and recommended config. Meridian to share trace logs and sample payloads for cache tuning.
topics: quantization impact on throughput and quality
hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs for cost predictability
transcript: [00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Alex from Redwood here, I'll kick us off. How's everybody doing?
[00:12] Jordan Lee: Hey Alex, good thanks. Busy week but ready to dig into the cost numbers.
[00:20] Priya Singh: Hi — Priya from Redwood infra, I'll be driving the benchmarking bits today.
[00:27] Maya Patel: Maya here, ML eng. we'll be looking at the tokens/sec and cache hits from our side.
[01:05] Alex Chen: Quick agenda: review the 2-week benchmark, walk through cost per unit, caching and batching tradeoffs, then action items. Is that good?
[01:30] Sam Torres: Sounds good, also want to touch on latency SLOs if we have time.

[02:10] Priya Singh: Cool. So last run we measured ~4,200 tokens/sec on the quantized 7B variant at a p95 latency around 240ms on our test harness; that translates to approx 0.023 tokens per dollar in the hosted baseline — oh wait, sorry, that was inverted, i mean 0.023 dollars per token? sorry, l-let me rephrase: roughly $0.000023 per token effectively when we account for batching and cache — transcription note: numbers rough
[02:45] Jordan Lee: Ok, can you repeat the tokens/sec per dollar? I think we reported tokens/sec/$ in the spreadsheet as 3.5k tokens per dollar for the hosted run?

[03:05] Priya Singh: Right — on hosted baseline without prefix caching we saw about 3,500 tokens per dollar. With KV/prefix caching enabled and a realistic prefix distribution from your sample payloads, that jumps to ~8k tokens per dollar. So caching is a big lever here.

[03:40] Maya Patel: That aligns with our logs; around 45% of requests share a common prefix so prefix caching should hit a lot. But our concern is correctness for some dynamic fields — we can't cache across user-specific tokens.

[04:05] Alex Chen: Totally. We usually implement selective prefix caching — keep user-specific segments out. For Meridian's flows, if we stash the product catalog + static prompt parts in KV cache it's safe and yields big savings.

[04:40] Priya Singh: Also batching: we found batch sizes of 8-12 give the best tokens/sec without pushing p95 too high. Above 16 the tail latency increases nonlinearly. So tradeoff — more batching reduces cost but can violate latency SLOs for interactive use.
[05:10] Jordan Lee: Our p95 SLO target is 300ms interactive, 500ms acceptable for background jobs. The batch 12 numbers are p95 ~260ms which is ok. What's the effect of quantization?

[05:30] Priya Singh: Quantization on the 7B variant moved throughput up ~1.4x and cost down roughly 30% at the hardware we used. There is slight quality delta in some long-context generative tests, but for your use-case the regression was within acceptable thresholds based on the eval set you shared.
[06:05] Maya Patel: Did you test 4-bit q or 8-bit? Our internal QA flagged hallucinations at 4-bit on long receipts.

[06:20] Priya Singh: We tested both; the 8-bit (nf4 8-bit-like) was stable; 4-bit had some edge regressions. Likely a tradeoff worth avoiding for the customer-facing generation until we have more prompt-level mitigation.

[07:00] Alex Chen: Important to call out: in dedicated mode with reserved capacity you'd get better tokens/sec/$ predictability and lower variance on latency, but cost commitment is higher. Any preference from Meridian?
[07:28] Jordan Lee: We're leaning hosted for the pilot to avoid up-front commit, but we want to know when dedicated becomes cost-effective. Do you have a break-even point?

[07:45] Priya Singh: Yes — in our model the break-even for a 7B quantized workload with your traffic profile is roughly 3 months at your projected request volume; we'll send a chart. We'll include sensitivity for cache hit rates and average sequence length.
[08:10] Sam Torres: On the SRE side, we'll need audit logs and KMS integration if we move to dedicated or private. Skipping for now but keep it in mind.
[09:00] Maya Patel: Back to caching — our sample payloads show about 35-50 token static prefix and then variable user text. How does Redwood's KV cache measure hit sizes?

[09:20] Priya Singh: Our KV cache stores prefix key to KV cache snapshot so if the first N tokens match cached prefix we get a full KV reuse and skip compute for first chunks; effective savings depend on prefix length and hit ratio. In your case with 45% shared prefixes and avg 40-token prefix, you get roughly 40% compute savings on average.
[10:05] Jordan Lee: Nice. Can you also simulate partial hits? Like 20-token prefix matches?

[10:20] Priya Singh: Yup, the model supports partial KV restore and we measured diminishing returns: a 20-token hit yields ~20% savings, 40-token hit ~40% — roughly linear until the attention overhead plateaus.
[11:00] Alex Chen: There's also caching TTL and eviction policies. Sam, from infra, do you have constraints on cache persistence?
[11:10] Sam Torres: We prefer cache to be short-lived per session; can't persist PII. TTL of a few hours max, and we need encryption at rest. Redwood supports those settings, yes?
[11:35] Alex Chen: Yes, we can configure TTL and KMS-backed encryption. We'll include that in the security docs we send.

[12:05] Priya Singh: Ok next I want to show the updated cost spreadsheet — (brief pause, link shared) — numbers here assume avg seq len 128 tokens, 45% cache hits, batch 10 for interactive. That yields ~7.8k tokens per dollar hosted, and dedicated reserved decreases unit cost by ~22% once amortized.
[12:45] Maya Patel: If we reduce seq len to 80 average for product search flows, how does that change?
[12:55] Priya Singh: Shorter sequences improve throughput significantly; tokens/sec goes up since KV cache also kicks more — effectively tokens per dollar goes up ~15-20% in that regime.
[13:20] Jordan Lee: Any concerns around cold start or burst behavior?

[13:30] Priya Singh: With prefix caching you can actually produce cold start savings once cache warmed; for bursts, autoscaling on hosted side does add slight latency bump, but we've built in fast warm mechanisms. Dedicated gives more stable tail latencies.

[14:10] Alex Chen: We also discussed a test matrix last week: run baseline, enable quantization, enable prefix cache, vary batch sizes. Are we agreed to run that again with your recent payload distribution?
[14:28] Maya Patel: Yes, we'll upload the distribution today — sending to the link in chat.
[14:40] Priya Singh: Great. For the next benchmark we'll also run a 1k concurrent request scenario to validate throughput under load — that'll inform dedicated sizing.
[15:05] Jordan Lee: Perfect. On the cost model, can you break out network egress and storage costs separately?
[15:20] Alex Chen: Yes — the spreadsheet will include compute, network egress, storage, and overhead (observability retention). We'll annotate assumptions for each.
[16:00] Sam Torres: One more ops question: how do you measure tokens — is it tokenization parity with our client? Sometimes tokenizers differ and token counts shift cost projections.

[16:20] Priya Singh: Good call — we tokenized using the same BPE vocab you provided; we'll share the tokenizer checksum and the tokenization script. Also we'll include a small utility to map your payloads to our tokenizer for sanity checks.
[17:05] Maya Patel: On quality — you mentioned eval regressions for 4-bit quant. Can you run a stability diff on our prompt set?
[17:20] Priya Singh: Yes, Priya will run the A/B with the pilot eval prompts and send a delta report.

[17:45] Alex Chen: Recap of action items: Redwood sends updated cost spreadsheet and quant results; Priya to recommend batching/KV settings; Meridian to share sample payloads and logs. Anyone disagree?
[18:00] Jordan Lee: Sounds right. Also we'll check internal procurement thresholds once we have break-even numbers.
[18:25] Maya Patel: Quick note—we have two special-case flows that cannot be cached; we'll flag those in the payload upload.
[19:05] Priya Singh: Noted. We'll exclude those from prefix caching simulation.
[20:00] Alex Chen: Ok last thing—competitive callouts: Jordan, you mentioned evaluating Vertex AI, Anthropic — any change there?
[20:15] Jordan Lee: We're still evaluating both; cost looks similar at scale but integration and compliance are big differentiators. Redwood's KV caching and rollout controls stood out for us.
[21:00] Alex Chen: Great. We'll send the security docs and a short note on dedicated break-even. Any other questions?
[21:20] Sam Torres: No, thanks all.
[21:30] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts. Meeting adjourned.
[21:35] (call ends)
